questions.q: What does 'serverless' mean for Athena specifically?
options: There is no cluster to provision or keep running; you query S3 data directly and pay only per query
Athena runs entirely on your own laptop with no AWS involvement
Athena requires you to manually launch an EC2 instance before each query
Athena has no servers anywhere, including AWS's own infrastructure
questions.explain: Athena has no user-managed cluster or standing infrastructure — AWS runs the query engine, and nothing is billed for compute between queries.

questions.q: What query engine family is Athena built on?
options: Presto, with much of the engine since migrated to Trino
A proprietary AWS-only engine unrelated to any open-source project
MySQL's query planner
Apache Hadoop MapReduce
questions.explain: Athena launched on Presto and has since migrated much of its execution engine to Trino, the community fork led by Presto's original creators.

options: By the amount of data scanned per query, regardless of query runtime
By a fixed hourly rate for a running cluster
By the number of tables in the Data Catalog
By the number of AWS Regions the query touches
questions.explain: Athena bills based on bytes scanned per query — not cluster uptime or query duration.

questions.q: Why does Athena support standard ANSI SQL with joins, aggregations, window functions, and CTEs?
options: Because it's built on Presto/Trino, a distributed SQL engine designed for querying data in place
Because AWS built a completely custom SQL dialect from scratch
It doesn't — Athena only supports simple SELECT statements
Because it converts every query into a Redshift Spectrum call first
questions.explain: Athena's Presto/Trino heritage is why it supports full ANSI SQL rather than a cut-down query dialect.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do two queries against the same dataset potentially cost different amounts?
options: One might scan far more bytes than the other (e.g. due to partitioning), and cost scales with bytes scanned, not query runtime
Athena charges more for queries submitted later in the day
Cost is identical for every query regardless of the data scanned
Only queries with joins are ever billed
questions.explain: Since Athena bills by bytes scanned, a poorly partitioned table that forces a full scan will cost more than a well-partitioned one for the same logical query.
